full_title: MARIA LINA P. QUIRIT-FIGARIDO, PETITIONER, VS. EDWIN L. FIGARIDO, RESPONDENT.
subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
syllabus_topic: III. Family Relations > A. Marriage > 4. Void and Voidable Marriages
topics: Who may file a petition to declare a bigamous marriage void (A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, Sec. 2(a))
The guilty spouse in a bigamous marriage has no personality to sue
Effect of a later foreign divorce on the prior spouse's standing
Judicial declaration of nullity is needed only for remarriage (Art. 40, Family Code)
Clean hands: no equity relief for the erring spouse

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > C. Parties to Civil Actions (Rule 3)

doctrine:
**Only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may file a petition to declare a bigamous marriage void. The spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage has no personality to file it.** Bigamous marriages are void ab initio under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. But under Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, a petition for declaration of absolute nullity "may be filed solely by the husband or the wife," and the Rationale of the Rule explains that "[o]nly an aggrieved or injured spouse" may file. Following *Juliano-Llave v. Republic* and *Fujiki v. Marinay*, the "husband or the wife" means the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage are neither husband nor wife in law. The En Banc applied these rules and jurisprudence to deny standing to the guilty spouse. Letting her sue would be a "legal absurdity": the offending spouse could dissolve the marriage at will and treat bigamy "as a matter of convenience."

A foreign divorce later obtained by the prior spouse ends that spouse's standing, since there is no longer a prior subsisting marriage. But it **does not pass the right to sue to the guilty spouse.** When the persons capable of filing are absent or disqualified, other parties do not automatically gain the right to attack the bigamous marriage. The State has no absolute duty to dissolve bigamous marriages, and the Court will not use its equity jurisdiction to free a party who willfully entered the void marriage and does not come with clean hands (*Alcantara v. Alcantara*).

The denial does not legalize the bigamous marriage. Under Article 40 of the Family Code, a judicial declaration of nullity is needed only for purposes of remarriage. For other purposes, such as heirship, legitimacy or illegitimacy of a child, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, or a criminal case, a court may rule on the marriage's validity in any case where the question is essential (*Cariño v. Cariño*). The erring parties also remain civilly and criminally liable for bigamy.
facts:
Maria Lina married Ho Kar Wai, a Chinese national, on December 13, 1989 in Hong Kong, and again on August 23, 1994 before a Metropolitan Trial Court judge in Parañaque City. In 2000 she met Edwin in Hong Kong. Edwin knew she had problems with her marital status, courted her anyway, and promised to wait until she settled them. While still married to Ho Kar Wai, Maria Lina had an affair with Edwin, became pregnant, and married him on February 22, 2003 in Quezon City. They had two children, born in 2004 and 2007.

On November 28, 2007, Ho Kar Wai obtained a divorce decree (Certificate of Making Decree Nisi Absolute) from the District Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. On Maria Lina's petition, the RTC of Parañaque City, Branch 260 recognized the foreign divorce in a Decision dated February 5, 2009.

Maria Lina and Edwin separated in 2014. On March 6, 2017, Maria Lina filed with a family court a petition to declare her marriage to Edwin void ab initio as bigamous under Article 35(4) of the Family Code, and to declare that she had the capacity to remarry. Edwin was served summons by publication and never appeared. At pre-trial, Edwin admitted that Maria Lina married him while her marriage to Ho Kar Wai was subsisting. Maria Lina admitted that she married Edwin before the RTC decision recognizing her divorce. She was the lone witness.

The family court denied the petition on August 30, 2019 and denied reconsideration. On appeal, the OSG argued that Maria Lina, as the party guilty of contracting the bigamous marriage, had no personality to file, because only the injured or aggrieved spouse may do so. The CA affirmed on June 21, 2021 and denied reconsideration on November 16, 2021. Maria Lina filed a Rule 45 petition. The OSG kept its position, and Edwin filed no comment.
issues: Whether Maria Lina, the spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage, has the personality to file a petition to declare her marriage to Edwin void ab initio for being bigamous.
Whether the Court may declare Maria Lina's marriage to Edwin void so that she may remarry, considering that her first husband has divorced her and that, she claims, no one else can file the petition.
ruling:
**1. No. Maria Lina has no personality to file the petition.** Article 35(4) of the Family Code declares bigamous marriages void ab initio. Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC provides that the petition "may be filed solely by the husband or the wife." Its Rationale states that "[o]nly an aggrieved or injured spouse may file petitions for annulment of voidable marriages and declaration of absolute nullity of void marriages." In *Juliano-Llave v. Republic*, the Court held that the prior spouse "is clearly the aggrieved party," because the bigamous marriage threatens the financial and property aspects of the prior marriage and places an emotional burden on the prior spouse. In *Fujiki v. Marinay*, it clarified that the "husband or the wife" in Section 2(a) is the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage "are neither the husband nor the wife under the law."

Maria Lina married Edwin in 2003 while her marriage to Ho Kar Wai subsisted. The divorce came only in 2007, and its recognition in 2009. She is guilty of contracting the bigamous marriage, so she cannot be an aggrieved or injured innocent spouse of either marriage. The Court rejected her attempt to distinguish *Juliano-Llave*, noting that the first wife was in fact one of the complainants there. Even if the divorce had ended the emotional and financial harm to the prior spouse, that would not make Maria Lina the aggrieved spouse. If anything, she benefited from the second union: she had two children with Edwin and filed only after 14 years. **Letting the erring spouse invoke the bigamous nature of her own marriage would produce a "legal absurdity": the offending spouse could dissolve the marriage at will and treat bigamy "as a matter of convenience."**

**2. No. The Court will not declare the marriage void at her instance.** Ho Kar Wai, the injured spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, had the right to file the petition. Once he obtained the divorce, however, there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage. He lost his status as the aggrieved spouse and can no longer file it. **The divorce "in no way resulted in the assignment of the right to petition" to Maria Lina.** Nothing in the rules or jurisprudence says that when the persons capable of filing are absent or disqualified, other concerned parties automatically gain the right to sue. The State has no absolute responsibility to dissolve bigamous marriages. The rules aim to preserve marriage, not to give guilty spouses "a convenient means to dissolve their illegitimate union." With no legitimate marriage left to protect, there is "no compelling reason for the State to dissolve her illegitimate marriage."

A judicial declaration of nullity matters only for remarriage. Under Article 40 of the Family Code, the marriage bond of a void marriage subsists only for that purpose. For other purposes (heirship, legitimacy, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, criminal cases), a court may rule on the validity of a marriage even in a suit not filed directly to question it (*Cariño v. Cariño*). Maria Lina's real goal was the capacity to remarry, and the law gives her no remedy for an inability "which she inflicted on herself." Following *Alcantara v. Alcantara*, the Court declined to use its equity jurisdiction for a party who willfully contracted the void marriage and does not come with clean hands.

The denial is not a refusal to declare the bigamous marriage void. It rejects only Maria Lina's personality to file the petition. It does not legalize bigamy: the erring parties may still be held civilly and criminally liable, and heirship, legitimacy, settlement of estate, and dissolution of the property regime may be resolved without a declaration of nullity.
disposition: The Petition for Review on Certiorari was DENIED. The CA Decision dated June 21, 2021 and Resolution dated November 16, 2021 in CA-G.R. CV No. 114777, which affirmed the family court's denial of the petition for declaration of nullity, were AFFIRMED.

bar_questions.q: In 1996, Liza married Kenji, a Japanese national, in Manila. In 2005, while still married to Kenji, Liza married Ramon, who knew of her existing marriage. They had three children. In 2009, Kenji obtained a valid divorce in Japan, which a Philippine RTC recognized in 2011. Liza and Ramon separated in 2016. In 2024, wanting to marry another man, Liza filed a petition to declare her marriage to Ramon void ab initio for being bigamous under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. The OSG opposed, arguing that Liza has no personality to file the petition. Liza replied that the marriage is admittedly bigamous and void, that Kenji can no longer sue because of the divorce, and that she is the only real party in interest left. Should the petition be granted?

alac.answer: No. The petition should be dismissed because Liza, the spouse who contracted the bigamous marriage, has no personality to file it.
alac.legal_basis: Bigamous marriages are void ab initio under Article 35(4) of the Family Code. Under Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, a petition for declaration of absolute nullity may be filed solely by the husband or the wife, which the Rationale of the Rule explains as the aggrieved or injured spouse. Only the aggrieved or injured innocent spouse may petition to declare a bigamous marriage void; the guilty spouse cannot. A foreign divorce later obtained by the prior spouse ends that spouse's standing but does not transfer the right to the guilty spouse. (Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido, G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc, applying Juliano-Llave v. Republic and Fujiki v. Marinay)
alac.application: Liza married Ramon in 2005 while her marriage to Kenji subsisted; the divorce came only in 2009. She is the guilty party, not an aggrieved or injured innocent spouse. Kenji was the injured spouse while the first marriage subsisted. After the divorce there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage, so he lost his standing, but his loss did not pass the right to Liza. That no one else can now file does not give her standing. The court will also not use equity to relieve a party who willfully contracted the bigamous marriage and benefited from it for years. Her real aim, the capacity to remarry, is a disability she brought on herself.
alac.conclusion: The petition should be dismissed because Liza has no personality to file it.

bar_questions.q: Liza, a Filipina, married Kenji, a Japanese national, in 1996. In 2005, while still married to Kenji, she married Ramon. In 2007, before any divorce, Kenji learned of the second marriage and filed in the Philippines a petition to declare the Liza-Ramon marriage void for being bigamous. Liza moved to dismiss, arguing that under A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC only "the husband or the wife" may file, and Kenji is not a party to her marriage with Ramon. (a) Does Kenji have personality to file the petition? (b) Would your answer be the same if Kenji filed the petition only in 2012, after his Japanese divorce from Liza had been recognized by a Philippine court?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Kenji, as the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, is the aggrieved party with personality to file. (b) No. After the divorce, Kenji no longer has standing to file the petition.
alac.legal_basis: Section 2(a) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, read with its Rationale, allows only the aggrieved or injured spouse to file. The "husband or the wife" in Section 2(a) refers to the spouse of the prior subsisting marriage, because the parties to a bigamous marriage are neither husband nor wife in law (Fujiki v. Marinay; Juliano-Llave v. Republic). In Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido (G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc), the Court held that the injured spouse of the prior subsisting marriage had the right to file the petition. Once he obtained a divorce decree, however, there was no longer a prior subsisting marriage, he lost his status as the aggrieved spouse, and he could no longer file it.
alac.application: (a) In 2007, Kenji's marriage to Liza was still subsisting. Her bigamous marriage threatened the property side of his marriage and caused him the emotional injury the rule protects against, so he is the aggrieved spouse and the proper party. Liza's reading would unjustly shut out the very spouse the rule is meant to protect. (b) By 2012, his marriage to Liza had been dissolved by a divorce recognized in the Philippines. With no prior subsisting marriage left to protect, he is no longer the aggrieved spouse and has lost the personality to file.
alac.conclusion: Kenji may file the petition while his marriage to Liza subsists, but not after his divorce from her.

bar_questions.q: Andrea married Carlos in 2010 while her marriage to Benjie was still subsisting. Benjie never sued. In 2023, Andrea's petition to declare her marriage to Carlos void was dismissed because, as the guilty spouse, she had no personality to file it. In 2025, Carlos died intestate. In the judicial settlement of his estate, Carlos's brother opposed Andrea's claim to inherit as surviving spouse, arguing that the marriage was bigamous and void. Andrea countered that no court has ever declared her marriage to Carlos void, and that the dismissal of her own petition means the marriage must be treated as valid. May the settlement court rule on the validity of Andrea's marriage to Carlos to determine Carlos's heirs?

alac.answer: Yes. The settlement court may rule on the validity of the marriage to determine heirship, even without a prior judicial declaration of nullity.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 40 of the Family Code, a judicial declaration of nullity of a previous marriage is required only for purposes of remarriage. For other purposes, such as heirship, legitimacy or illegitimacy of a child, settlement of estate, dissolution of the property regime, or a criminal case, a court may rule on the validity of a marriage even after the parties' death and even in a suit not filed directly to question it, so long as the question is essential to the case (Cariño v. Cariño). In Quirit-Figarido v. Figarido (G.R. No. 259520, November 5, 2024, En Banc), the Court stressed that denying the guilty spouse's petition for lack of personality is not a refusal to declare the bigamous marriage void and does not legalize it. These incidents may proceed without a declaration of nullity, and the erring parties remain civilly and criminally liable for bigamy.
alac.application: The dismissal of Andrea's petition rested only on her lack of personality. It did not hold that her marriage to Carlos was valid. Whether Andrea is Carlos's surviving spouse is essential to determining his heirs, so the settlement court may examine whether the marriage was celebrated while her marriage to Benjie subsisted. If it was, the marriage is void under Article 35(4) of the Family Code, and Andrea cannot claim to be Carlos's surviving spouse.
alac.conclusion: The settlement court may rule on the validity of the marriage to determine Carlos's heirs, despite the absence of a judicial declaration of nullity.

notes: En Banc vote: Inting, M. Lopez, J. Lopez, Dimaampao, Marquez and Kho, Jr., JJ. concurred. Gesmundo, C.J., Caguioa, J. and Singh, J. wrote concurring opinions. Lazaro-Javier and Zalameda, JJ. dissented; Leonen, SAJ. joined both dissents, and Hernando, J. (on official business) joined Justice Lazaro-Javier's dissent. Gaerlan, J. was on official leave. The separate opinions, which make up most of the cached text, are not examinable and were not used. The children's names are redacted in the decision. The Court did not decide whether the second husband, Edwin, could file the petition; it only noted Maria Lina's claim that he could not.
